subject: MGMT464
title: Hurdle 7 · The Village of Silence — Leadership of Culture, Ethics and Diversity

questions.stem: Describe organisational culture.
options: The aggregate of beliefs, norms, attitudes, values, assumptions and ways of doing things shared by members and taught to new members
The list of rules in the handbook
The national culture of the owner
questions.why: Culture. See §7.1.

questions.stem: Identify the two functions culture serves.
questions.why: Both are about power. See §7.1.

questions.stem: Identify the three levels where culture lives.
options: Artefacts, espoused values and basic assumptions
questions.why: Schein's levels as used in the textbook. See §7.1.

questions.stem: Explain how leaders change basic assumptions.
options: Only by changing what they do at the first two levels — artefacts and espoused values
By writing a new mission statement
questions.why: Leaders change the third level only by changing what they do. See §7.1.

questions.stem: Differentiate a strong culture from a weak one.
options: Strong: values widely shared and intensely held; weak: little agreement, subcultures with different values
Strong: big company; weak: small company
Strong: many rules; weak: few rules
questions.why: Strength. See §7.2.

questions.stem: Explain the point most managers miss about strong cultures.
options: A strong culture is only an asset when it fits the strategy and the environment — strength is not fit
questions.why: Strength is not the same as fit. See §7.2.

questions.stem: Describe the strong-culture trap.
options: When the environment changes and the culture does not, its strength becomes speed in the wrong direction
A strong culture hires too many people
questions.why: Answer to question 2. See §7.2.

questions.stem: Identify the diagnostic for culture strength.
options: Ask three people what the organisation values most — the same answer means strong; fit is a separate question
questions.why: Diagnostic for your Project 2 organisation. See §7.2.

questions.stem: Describe symbolic actions.
options: Signals — what the leader pays attention to, measures and rewards; reactions to crises; stories and heroes; rituals; the leader's own visible behaviour
questions.why: Symbols are cheap and powerful. See §7.3.

questions.stem: Describe substantive actions.
options: Changing the systems so values are enforced — hiring for fit, promotion criteria, structure, policies, training, removing violators, budget
questions.why: Substantive actions make the symbols credible. See §7.3.

questions.stem: Explain what happens when symbolic and substantive actions disagree.
options: Followers believe the reward system, not the speech — the talk becomes decoration
questions.why: Chapter 3's reinforcement principle for a whole organisation. See §7.3.

questions.stem: Identify Sheri McCoy's substantive actions at Avon.
options: Replacing executives, restructuring markets, cooperating with the investigation
questions.why: Symbolic vs substantive at Avon. See §7.3.

questions.stem: Identify the two dimensions behind the four culture types.
options: Need for flexibility or stability, and strategic focus internal or external
questions.why: Four types result. See §7.4.

questions.stem: Describe the adaptive culture.
options: External focus, flexibility — values entrepreneurship, innovation, risk-taking and responsiveness; risk of chaos
Internal focus, stability — values rules and predictability
Internal focus, flexibility — values people and teamwork
External focus, stability — values winning and results
questions.why: Adaptive. See §7.4.

questions.stem: Identify the culture type that fits regulated, safety-critical or high-volume routine work.
questions.why: Bureaucratic — risk: cannot adapt. See §7.4.

questions.stem: Identify the risk of a competitive culture.
questions.why: Competitive. See §7.4.

questions.stem: Identify Hofstede's five dimensions used in the chapter.
options: Individualism–collectivism, uncertainty avoidance, power distance, masculinity–femininity, long-term–short-term orientation
questions.why: Five dimensions in a GCC workplace. See §7.5.

questions.stem: Describe the leadership implication of high power distance.
options: Staff will not challenge you in a meeting — ask privately and individually or you will hear only agreement
questions.why: Power distance. See §7.5.

questions.stem: Describe what high uncertainty avoidance members want.
options: Written procedures and clear roles before they act — and an explanation when you deviate
questions.why: Uncertainty avoidance. See §7.5.

questions.stem: Explain the leader's job in a multinational team, in the chapter's words.
options: Not to average the cultures but to make the team's norms explicit so nobody has to guess
questions.why: Answer to question 3. See §7.5.

questions.stem: Identify the practices that foster an ethical work environment.
options: Code of ethics, ethics committee and ombudsperson, training, disclosure mechanisms, leaders as role models, reward and punishment aligned
questions.why: The leader is in every one. See §7.6.

questions.stem: Identify the least effective item on the list, when alone.
questions.why: Necessary — and alone, the least effective. See §7.6.

questions.stem: Explain why scandals happen inside organisations with codes.
options: Role-modelling and reward alignment were missing — the leader modelled the opposite, or results excused the method
questions.why: Answer to question 4. See §7.6.

questions.stem: Identify the four components of authentic leadership.
options: Self-awareness, relational transparency, balanced processing, internalised moral perspective
questions.why: Authentic leadership. See §7.7.

questions.stem: Describe one of the three limits of 'being yourself'.
options: It is not an excuse for staying the same — a short temper is a habit, not an identity
Authenticity is the same in every culture
questions.why: Three limits. See §7.7.

questions.stem: Explain why authentic leadership sits in the culture chapter.
options: An authentic leader is the strongest symbolic action a culture can have — the person whose behaviour matches the code
questions.why: Why it sits with culture. See §7.7.

questions.stem: Identify the benefits of diversity the textbook argues from performance.
options: Better decisions, creativity, access to diverse markets, a wider talent pool, adaptability, legal and reputational protection
questions.why: Argued from performance, not only fairness. See §7.8.

questions.stem: Identify the leadership actions that sustain a pro-diversity culture.
options: Top-management commitment, diversity as a strategy with goals, fair recruitment/promotion/pay systems, training, mentoring and networks, accountability
Hiring one person from each country
questions.why: A pro-diversity culture is an outcome of leadership. See §7.8.

questions.stem: Describe the UAE frame for diversity.
options: Some 200 nationalities; a Labour Law that prohibits discrimination and requires equal pay; Emiratisation and gender-balance policies
questions.why: Diversity here is not a choice — leadership of it is. See §7.8.

questions.stem: Identify the new form of exclusion to watch in hybrid work.
questions.why: What globalisation adds. See §7.8.

questions.stem: Explain the chapter's reading of Avon in question 1.
options: Strong internally (espoused values) but weak externally — a culture built around one model failed to adapt, and assumptions in some markets diverged from the values
questions.why: Answer to question 1. See §7.1.

questions.stem: Identify the culture type that values people, participation, trust and teamwork.
questions.why: Cooperative — risk: consensus slows decisions. See §7.4.

questions.stem: Exercise 1A: a federal service centre — every step documented, promotions by seniority, nobody deviates from the manual — with a mandate to move 80% of services online in a year. Determine the culture type, its strength and its fit.
options: Bureaucratic, strong, no longer fits — it needs an adaptive culture
questions.why: Answer key: A bureaucratic, strong, no longer fits. See §7.4 and Exercise 1.

questions.stem: Exercise 1B: a Sharjah tech start-up — decisions in the corridor, failures celebrated, the CEO codes; three products launched, one kept. Determine the culture type and fit.
questions.why: Answer key: B adaptive, fits. See §7.4 and Exercise 1.

questions.stem: Exercise 1C: a family retail group — forty-year employees, birthdays celebrated, decisions by consensus — and a competitor undercutting prices by 20%. Determine the type, strength and fit.
options: Cooperative, strong, fit under threat — it needs competitive elements
questions.why: Answer key: C cooperative, strong, fit under threat. See §7.4 and Exercise 1.

questions.stem: Exercise 1D: the Indian engineers never contradict the Emirati manager in meetings, the British analyst does constantly, and the manager thinks the engineers agree. Determine the Hofstede dimension and two leader behaviours.
options: Power distance (and collectivism); ask individually or privately and ask for written input before meetings, explicitly inviting disagreement
questions.why: Answer key: D power distance. See §7.5 and Exercise 1.

questions.stem: Exercise 1E: a bank with the code of ethics on every wall, whose top seller was promoted despite two mis-selling complaints. Determine the practices present and the failure that makes the code decoration.
options: Code present; reward misaligned — promotion despite complaints — so symbolic and substantive actions disagree
questions.why: Answer key: E reward misaligned. See §7.6, §7.3 and Exercise 1.

questions.stem: Exercise 2, the depot: a 'family' culture with a code of ethics, and a star supervisor who allocates overtime by nationality, ignores grievances and altered a log. Determine the espoused values and the basic assumption revealed.
options: Espoused: family and the ethics code; assumption: results and loyalty to the founder excuse conduct
questions.why: Marking guide, task 1. See §7.1 and Exercise 2.

questions.stem: Exercise 2: determine whether the depot's strong 'family' culture is an asset or the trap.
options: The trap — it protects the protégé and silences complaint
An asset — it keeps staff loyal
An asset — the depot is fastest
questions.why: Marking guide, task 1. See §7.2 and Exercise 2.

questions.stem: Exercise 2: determine which ethical practices exist on paper and which failed in practice.
options: Code and grievance procedure exist; disclosure/protection, role-modelling and reward alignment have failed
questions.why: Marking guide, task 2. See §7.6 and Exercise 2.

questions.stem: Exercise 2: determine what 'fix it quietly' teaches the culture, and the actions that would make the code real.
options: It teaches that results excuse everything; investigate formally, apply the same standard as to anyone, publish the outcome principle, tie supervisor pay to fairness metrics
questions.why: Marking guide, task 2. See §7.3 and Exercise 2.

questions.stem: Exercise 2: determine the Hofstede dimensions that explain 'that is just how it is here'.
questions.why: Marking guide, task 3. See §7.5 and Exercise 2.

questions.stem: Exercise 2: select three leadership actions that would rebuild a pro-diversity culture in the depot.
options: Transparent overtime and promotion criteria, mentoring for under-represented staff, managers measured on inclusion (plus awareness training and a protected channel)
A diversity poster, a lunch and a speech
Move the supervisor to another depot quietly
questions.why: Marking guide, task 3. See §7.8 and Exercise 2.

questions.stem: Exercise 2, the position: select the response the marking guide describes as a defended position.
options: Formal investigation; a sanction proportionate to the falsified log and the discrimination; a respectful but firm reply to the founder citing the law and the culture cost — with the strongest objection answered
Do nothing and keep the depot fast
Quietly move the supervisor and say nothing
questions.why: Marking guide, task 4: reward the argument, not the side. See §7.6 and Exercise 2.

questions.stem: Exercise 2: Determine the stakeholders the decision affects.
options: Staff who left and stayed, the supervisor, the founder, customers, and the company's legal exposure
questions.why: Marking guide, task 4. See §7.6 and Exercise 2.

questions.stem: Exercise 2: Determine the strongest objection to a formal investigation, and the answer.
options: 'We lose the best depot' — answered by the law, the staff already leaving, and what every other depot learns from the decision
'It is expensive' — answered by the budget
questions.why: Strongest objection answered. See §7.6 and Exercise 2.

questions.stem: Take-away: a student records the office layout, the dress code and the story told to new joiners. Determine the level of culture observed.
options: Artefacts — and the story reveals the value it teaches
questions.why: Take-away box 1. See §7.1.

questions.stem: Take-away: the leader visibly praises customer care, but promotions in the last three years went only to the biggest cost-cutters. Determine the finding.
options: A gap between symbolic and substantive actions — usually the most interesting finding in the report
questions.why: Take-away box 3. See §7.3.

questions.stem: Take-away: the student notices no women and only two nationalities at the top of a 30-nationality company. Determine the section it belongs to and the reading.
options: Ethics and inclusion — who gets the visible work and promotions; a pro-diversity culture is not being sustained
questions.why: Take-away box 4. See §7.8.

questions.stem: In the village, nobody will tell Rami in public that his plan is wrong; they tell Noor privately. Determine the dimension and what Rami should do.
options: High power distance — ask individually and privately, and reward the first disagreement
questions.why: Ask privately or you will hear only agreement. See §7.5.

questions.stem: Rami preaches fairness but gives the best horse to his cousin every time. Determine what the village learns.
options: That the talk is decoration — followers believe the reward system, not the speech
questions.why: Symbolic and substantive actions must agree. See §7.3.

questions.stem: The village has done things 'the way the elders did' for a century; it worked until the gang arrived. Determine the chapter's name for the problem.
options: The strong-culture trap — strength became speed in the wrong direction
questions.why: Answer to question 2. See §7.2.

questions.stem: Rami admits to the village that he is afraid, explains what he knows and what he does not, and decides against the elders' pressure because the plan is wrong. Classify the components shown.
options: Authentic leadership — relational transparency, balanced processing, internalised moral perspective
questions.why: Four components. See §7.7.

questions.stem: The rescue party is four people of different villages, ages and skills; Noor says that is why they see what the gang misses. Determine the benefit of diversity she describes.
options: Better decisions — more perspectives and fewer blind spots
questions.why: Benefits of diversity. See §7.8.

questions.stem: Omar reports that a village guard took a bribe from the gang; the elders punish Omar for 'making trouble'. Determine the ethical-environment practice that failed.
options: Disclosure mechanisms — a channel to report wrongdoing without retaliation
questions.why: Report without retaliation. See §7.6.

questions.stem: The village council wants rules for everything and promotes the oldest; the gang runs on raids, risk and quick decisions. Classify the two cultures.
options: Village: bureaucratic; gang: adaptive (with competitive elements)
questions.why: Four types. See §7.4.

questions.stem: Describe the role of an ethics committee and ombudsperson.
options: A body that interprets the code, hears cases and protects the person who reports
questions.why: Ethics committee and ombudsperson. See §7.6.

questions.stem: Identify the component of authentic leadership that matches Chapter 2's postconventional level.
options: Internalised moral perspective — behaviour guided by internal standards rather than group or organisational pressure
questions.why: Internalised moral perspective. See §7.7.

questions.stem: Analyse the village's story about the elder who gave his own horse to a stranger — told to every child. Determine the level of culture and what it teaches.
options: An artefact (a story) that teaches the value of hospitality — artefacts carry values
An espoused value in the code
questions.why: Where culture lives. See §7.1.

questions.stem: Determine the function of culture that lets two villagers who never met act the same way when the gang appears.
options: Internal unity — culture coordinates people who never meet
questions.why: Internal unity. See §7.1.

questions.stem: Rami asks three villagers what the village values most; all three say 'loyalty to the elders'. Determine the reading and the follow-up question.
options: Strong culture — then ask whether loyalty to the elders still fits a valley under attack
questions.why: Same answer = strong; fit is a separate question. See §7.2.

questions.stem: Analyse a village whose every family does things differently and whose newcomers never 'get it'. Classify the culture and its risk.
options: Weak — drift and no shared direction, but easier to change
questions.why: Weak culture. See §7.2.

questions.stem: Rami eats with the lowest-ranked scouts every evening and asks the youngest's opinion first. Classify the action.
options: Symbolic — the leader's visible behaviour signals what the culture values
questions.why: Symbolic actions. See §7.3.

questions.stem: Rami's temper flares at every setback; he says 'that is just who I am'. Determine the chapter's reply.
options: 'Being yourself' is not an excuse for staying the same — a short temper is a habit, not an identity
questions.why: Three limits. See §7.7.

questions.stem: Rami gathers all views — including the ones against his plan — before deciding. Classify the component.
questions.why: Objectively analysing all relevant data. See §7.7.

questions.stem: Dana shows strong emotion in the village council and is called unprofessional; in her home village it would be honest. Determine the chapter's point.
options: 'Authentic' means different things in different cultures — which matters in a Gulf workplace
questions.why: Three limits. See §7.7.

questions.stem: Omar wants written rules for every crossing before he will move; Noor is happy to improvise. Determine the Hofstede dimension.
questions.why: High-avoidance members want written procedures. See §7.5.

questions.stem: The elders refuse to let women or outsiders join the guard. Determine the chapter's performance argument against this.
options: It narrows the talent pool, loses perspectives and creates blind spots — diversity improves decisions
questions.why: The benefits argued from performance. See §7.8.
